query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of Nb during alloy synthesis will lead to the in situ formation of nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates that enhance the creep resistance, high-temperature stability, and corrosion behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy while preserving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure.
generation.intervention: Add a small quantity of Nb during the alloy fabrication process to promote the formation of Nb-rich nanoprecipitates.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be evaluated under aerospace-relevant conditions including cyclic temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (with tests for room-temperature creep and high-temperature behavior), and corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates that form along grain boundaries and within the lamellar matrix.
generation.mechanism: The Nb-rich precipitates are expected to serve as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding. This impediment improves resistance to creep deformation and stabilizes the microstructure under fluctuating temperatures, while also contributing to a more robust passive film that enhances corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Nb-modified alloy is predicted to exhibit improved creep resistance, enhanced high-temperature stability, and better corrosion performance without sacrificing its balanced strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The performance characteristics of the unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only within a narrow range of Nb addition; excessive Nb could lead to undesired phase formation and embrittlement. The improvements are limited to the environmental and mechanical conditions representative of aerospace applications.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvements and the optimal Nb concentration require further experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and a second set with a controlled, small Nb addition. Subject both sets to a series of tests including high-temperature and room-temperature creep tests, cyclic thermal fluctuation tests, and accelerated corrosion evaluations. Employ microstructural characterization techniques (e.g., TEM, SEM, XRD) to confirm the formation and distribution of Nb-rich precipitates.
measurements: Creep strain rate and total strain accumulation under sustained load
Microstructural analysis of precipitate size and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-modified samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in creep resistance, high-temperature stability, and corrosion behavior, or if there is a marked loss in strength–ductility balance compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Applying a targeted aging heat treatment to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will induce a fine, uniform dispersion of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates that simultaneously improve strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion performance under cyclic temperature conditions.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure.
drafts.intervention: A carefully controlled aging heat treatment (i.e., solution treatment followed by isothermal aging at an optimized temperature range) designed to precipitate uniformly distributed nanoscale intermetallic phases.
drafts.conditions: The treatment should be performed in an inert atmosphere, with the isothermal aging temperature set in the range of approximately 600–700°C for a duration sufficient to nucleate and grow fine precipitates without coarsening; this process is to be applied uniformly to samples intended for extreme service conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates located at or near the lamellar boundaries that can act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding.
drafts.mechanism: The precipitates provide additional barriers to dislocation motion, enhancing strength and ductility, while also impeding creep deformation under long-term mechanical loading and stabilizing the microstructure against degradation during temperature fluctuations. They may also foster a more protective surface microstructure that improves corrosion resistance under harsh environments.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast alloy, the heat-treated alloy is expected to exhibit a significant improvement in mechanical performance (e.g., increased tensile strength and ductility, reduced room-temperature creep rate) and enhanced corrosion resistance when subjected to cyclic temperature fluctuations.
drafts.baseline: Performance metrics obtained from the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with its existing fine lamellar structure.
drafts.boundary: The benefits of the intervention depend on precise control of the aging temperature and time; deviations might result in either insufficient precipitate formation or excessive coarsening, which could negate or even impair the desired improvements. The alloy’s response under conditions significantly outside the tested temperature and loading ranges remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one set will undergo the proposed aging heat treatment and the second set will be retained in the as-cast condition. Both sets will then be subjected to mechanical tests (tensile strength, ductility tests, room-temperature creep measurements) and corrosion tests (such as salt spray testing) under cyclic temperature conditions that simulate service environments.
measurements: Creep rate under constant load at room temperature
Corrosion rate (mass loss or electrochemical measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 10% enhancement in tensile strength and ductility, a measurable reduction in creep rate, and improved corrosion resistance) compared to the as-cast samples under identical test conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Nb to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy will induce the in situ formation of stable, nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates that improve the alloy’s high-temperature creep resistance and corrosion stability while maintaining a satisfactory strength–ductility balance.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure currently showing suboptimal performance under long-term mechanical loading and corrosive/high-temperature cycling.
drafts.intervention: Introduce 1–3 atomic percent Nb during alloy synthesis to promote nano-precipitation during solidification/aging.
drafts.conditions: Evaluate performance under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (including room-temperature creep tests), and corrosive environments representative of aircraft and spacecraft fastener service conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of finely dispersed Nb-rich precipitates along lamellar interfaces and/or at grain boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: The Nb-rich precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby reducing creep deformation under long-term load. Simultaneously, these precipitates help stabilize the microstructure and may serve as barriers to corrosion pathways, contributing to improved chemical durability under fluctuating temperatures and corrosive conditions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: An alloy with enhanced high-temperature and long-term mechanical stability (notably improved creep resistance) and superior corrosion resistance, while retaining a strength–ductility balance comparable to or better than the baseline alloy.
drafts.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with a fine lamellar structure.
drafts.boundary: The improvements are expected only within a narrow Nb-addition window (around 1–3 atomic percent); excess Nb may lead to embrittlement or other undesired phase formations. The effect may also depend on the specific test environments and exact processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys with varying Nb content (e.g., 0%, 1%, 2%, 3%) using identical melting and processing conditions. Subject the samples to standardized high-temperature creep tests (e.g., creep tests at 600°C for prolonged durations), cyclic thermal fluctuation tests, and accelerated corrosion tests in a representative corrosive medium. Use microstructural characterization (TEM, SEM, XRD) to confirm the formation and distribution of Nb-rich precipitates.
measurements: Creep strain rate and time to failure under constant load at high temperature
Electrochemical corrosion current density and potential
Microstructural analysis (size, distribution, and phase identification of precipitates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if samples with Nb addition do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in creep resistance and corrosion stability, or if the strength–ductility balance is compromised (e.g., substantial loss of ductility) compared to the baseline. Similarly, if Nb-rich precipitates do not form under the proposed processing conditions, the hypothesis is challenged.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition (≈1–2 at%) of Nb into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy will lead to the controlled formation of Nb-rich nanoprecipitates that enhance high-temperature stability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion behavior while preserving its balanced strength–ductility performance.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure
drafts.intervention: Add a small amount (around 1–2 atomic percent) of Nb during alloy fabrication
drafts.conditions: Evaluated under aerospace-relevant conditions including cyclic temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (to simulate creep at room and high temperatures) and corrosive environments
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of stable, coherent Nb-rich nanoprecipitates that are distributed within the lamellar matrix and along the grain boundaries
drafts.mechanism: Nb atoms segregate during solidification and subsequent processing to form finely distributed precipitates. These nanoprecipitates act to pin dislocations, reduce strain localization and retard grain-boundary sliding under long-term loading, thus improving creep resistance and high-temperature stability. Additionally, their presence may help in forming a more robust passive layer, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance without compromising the ductility provided by the lamellar structure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Nb-doped alloy should exhibit improved creep resistance, better high-temperature stability and enhanced corrosion resistance while maintaining or slightly improving its strength–ductility balance.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective if the Nb addition does not lead to excessive formation of brittle intermetallic phases that could deteriorate ductility or compromise the fine lamellar structure; improvements should be verified under realistic aerospace loading and environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and another set with 1–2 at% Nb addition. Subject both sets to a series of tests including cyclic high-temperature loading, room-temperature and high-temperature creep tests, and corrosion tests in aggressive environments that simulate aerospace conditions. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to analyze the microstructural evolution and precipitate formation in the Nb-added samples.
measurements: Creep rate and strain accumulation under long-term loading at room and elevated temperatures
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility measurements
Corrosion potential, corrosion rate and passive film integrity assessments
Microstructural characterization including size, distribution, and coherence of Nb-rich precipitates via TEM/SEM and phase identification via XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in creep resistance, high-temperature stability, or corrosion behavior, or if there is a pronounced loss of ductility or unexpected embrittlement relative to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Integrating a controlled trace addition of yttrium into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will form stable nanoparticle dispersoids that simultaneously improve strength, ductility, and durability under extreme conditions.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a minor (~<1 wt%) yttrium addition during alloy processing to promote the in situ formation of yttrium-rich nanoparticle dispersoids.
drafts.conditions: Process the alloy under conventional casting followed by a controlled thermal treatment designed to encourage dispersoid formation without triggering excessive formation of brittle intermetallic phases.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoparticle dispersoids (e.g., yttrium oxides or yttrium-rich precipitates) that pin grain boundaries and act as barriers to dislocation motion.
drafts.mechanism: The yttrium-induced dispersoids are expected to obstruct dislocation movement (dispersion strengthening) and inhibit grain boundary coarsening during high-temperature exposure, thereby improving both the strength–ductility balance and the alloy’s resistance to creep and corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: An improved mechanical performance with an estimated enhancement (potentially around 10–20%, though exact gains remain uncertain) in yield strength and ductility, alongside better stability under cyclic thermal load, creep conditions, and corrosive environments compared to the baseline alloy.
drafts.baseline: The performance characteristics of the unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy that exhibits a fine lamellar structure.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is effective only if the yttrium content remains low enough (<1 wt%) to avoid forming brittle intermetallic compounds; additionally, the thermal treatment must be optimized to promote dispersoid refinement without triggering detrimental phase transformations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one group of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and another group with a controlled yttrium addition (<1 wt%). Process both groups under identical casting and thermal treatment protocols. Conduct mechanical tests (tensile and creep testing), along with corrosion resistance evaluation, under accelerated aging and thermal fluctuation conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-modified samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., at least a 10% increase in yield strength and ductility, along with measurable enhancements in creep and corrosion resistance) over the baseline alloy, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
